report:
## Conclusion

The evidence suggests vegetarian diets are associated with modest reductions in mortality risk, but the claim that they clearly "increase life expectancy compared with eating meat" is only partially supported and comes with important caveats.

**What the evidence shows:**

- Large cohort studies of Seventh-day Adventists (a population with high rates of vegetarianism) found that vegetarian diets were associated with lower all-cause mortality, particularly in men, in the Adventist Health Study 2 (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/1710093).
- A broader Australian cohort study of over 267,000 people similarly examined vegetarian diets and all-cause mortality (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0091743516304479), though findings across such studies are mixed once adjusted for other lifestyle factors (exercise, smoking, alcohol use, BMI) common among vegetarians.
- A 2021 meta-analysis found vegetarian diets reduced risk of death from ischemic heart disease specifically, but had **no significant effect on all-cause mortality**, and the researchers rated the certainty of evidence as low (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/).
- A review of long-term vegetarian/vegan health outcomes concluded that "overall mortality is similar for vegetarians and comparable non-vegetarians," though vegetarians fare better than the general population, likely due to healthier lifestyles overall (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-nutrition-society/article/longterm-health-of-vegetarians-and-vegans/263822873377096A7BAC4F887D42A4CA).

**Bottom line:** Vegetarian diets are linked to reduced risk of certain causes of death (especially cardiovascular disease) and better health markers, but rigorous meta-analyses show inconsistent or low-certainty effects on overall (all-cause) mortality/life expectancy. Much of the apparent benefit may reflect confounding with other healthy behaviors common among vegetarians rather than diet alone. The claim is plausible but not conclusively proven by current evidence.
